<reflection>
- The previous experiment (high S, low cat) successfully penalized models with first-order or substrate-induced deactivation of the catalyst-substrate complex (M14, M16, and M20 dropped significantly in likelihood). 
- However, my aim to completely break the degeneracy was only partially achieved. The top models (M12, M18, M19, M2, M1) are still tightly clustered with NLLs around -63. The differences between product-induced deactivation (M12), bimolecular deactivation (M18, M19), catalyst dimerization (M2), and standard Michaelis-Menten (M1) remain too small to confidently select a single mechanism.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To strongly differentiate the remaining top candidates, we need an experiment that maximizes the divergence between their specific structural dependencies. By using a low substrate concentration (S=0.2), a high catalyst concentration (cat=0.15), and the maximum initial product concentration (P=0.5), we create an environment dominated by free catalyst (`cat`) and product (`P`), with very little catalyst-substrate complex (`catS`).
1. If M12 (P + cat => inactive) is the true mechanism, the abundance of both P and free `cat` will cause rapid, immediate deactivation, stalling the reaction almost instantly.
2. If M17 (P + catS => inactive) or M18 (2catS => inactive) are true, deactivation will be minimal because `catS` is scarce. The reaction will proceed much further than in M12.
3. If M19 (cat + catS => inactive) is true, deactivation will occur at a moderate rate, distinct from both M12 and M18.
4. If M2 (2cat <=> cat2) is true, the high concentration of free `cat` will strongly drive dimerization, altering the apparent catalytic rate compared to the standard M1 model.
This design avoids the saturation regime and specifically targets the vulnerabilities of the top competing hypotheses by manipulating the ratio of free `cat` to `catS` in a high-product environment.
</hypothesis>
